recent_posts.title: Why are the Artemis II photos on Flickr?
recent_posts.summary: NASA shares Artemis II mission photos on Flickr rather than its own website, and this post explains the historical and philosophical reasons why. Flickr, founded in 2004, pioneered high-resolution photo storage, Creative Commons licensing, and user data ownership during the Web 2.0 era. After passing through Yahoo and Verizon, it was acquired by SmugMug, which created the Flickr Foundation with a 100-year plan to preserve public digital archives in partnership with the U.S. Library of Congress. Flickr's combination of full-resolution storage, explicit public domain licensing, and long-term institutional commitment makes it uniquely suited for preserving historically significant government imagery — especially as current political pressures threaten the integrity of official government websites and public records.

recent_posts.title: CorridorKey shows ethical AI is possible with open source green screen tool
recent_posts.summary: Anil Dash highlights CorridorKey, an open-source AI tool for green screen keying created by Corridor Digital's Niko Pueringer, as an example of ethical AI done right. The tool was trained on consensually gathered synthetic data, is fully open source with open weights, runs on consumer hardware, and imposes no surveillance or restrictions on users. Within days of release, the community improved usability and reduced hardware requirements dramatically. Dash argues this proves that the harmful behaviors of Big AI companies — non-consensual training data, closed models, environmental recklessness — are deliberate choices, not technical necessities. He sees purpose-built, community-driven, under-hyped AI tools as a viable alternative to one-size-fits-all commercial platforms.

recent_posts.title: Ten years of writing about Prince collected in one place
recent_posts.summary: A retrospective marking ten years since Prince's death, curating Anil Dash's writings, podcast appearances, and archival work about Prince. Highlights include a minute-by-minute breakdown of how Purple Rain was created, an analysis of Prince's Super Bowl halftime show as a statement on race and legacy, recovered digital artifacts from Prince's early websites (including his personal liner notes and a letter explaining his name change), and a floppy disk recovery of the Prince symbol font. Also points to the Prince Online Museum, a fan spreadsheet cataloging thousands of Prince recordings, and a talk Dash delivered in Minneapolis connecting Prince's artistic independence to themes of immigration and systemic power.

recent_posts.title: How AI is triggering a software security crisis comparable to Y2K
recent_posts.summary: LLMs are rapidly accelerating the discovery and exploitation of software security vulnerabilities, creating a crisis analogous to Y2K. AI coding agents can find hundreds of times more vulnerabilities than previous tools, chain them together in novel ways, and enable highly personalized attacks at scale. Open source projects face a double threat: being flooded with AI-generated slop code submissions while simultaneously having their codebases scanned for exploits. The US regulatory response is hampered by political dysfunction, leaving the burden on private sector collaboration, academia, and local governments. The author argues that every substantial codebase in production today should be assumed exploitable, and that fundamental assumptions about software development, code sharing, and trust in the supply chain must change.

recent_posts.title: People want to work hard when given purpose and autonomy
recent_posts.summary: The narrative that employees don't want to work hard is a myth perpetuated by executives and media. People are intrinsically motivated when given a clear mission, shared values, autonomy, and mutual trust. When teams underperform, the root cause is almost always poor leadership, dehumanizing work conditions, lack of agency, inadequate tools, or misaligned goals — not laziness. Leaders who create the right environment and get out of the way will find their teams over-deliver. The cynical view of worker motivation reveals a failure of leadership imagination, not a flaw in workers.

recent_posts.title: On the Vergecast, On Video
recent_posts.summary: Anil Dash appeared on The Vergecast podcast to discuss Apple's moves around video podcasts and the broader importance of keeping podcasts open. The conversation was grounded in the idea that the phrase 'Wherever you get your podcasts' represents a radical commitment to openness. The episode also features Jason Snell reflecting on Apple's 50th anniversary, including commentary on the company's recent moral failures.

recent_posts.title: Defending Privacy, Daily
recent_posts.summary: Anil Dash, an EFF board member, shares his experience accompanying EFF executive director Cindy Cohn to The Daily Show, where she discussed digital privacy and civil liberties. He highlights Cohn's new book 'Privacy's Defender' from MIT Press, covering her 30-year fight against digital surveillance, and calls on readers to support the EFF amid growing threats from government overreach and big tech. He also announces a public conversation with Cohn at the Brooklyn Public Library on April 23.

recent_posts.title: What happens to software developers as AI takes over coding
recent_posts.summary: Anil Dash reflects on what AI-powered coding tools mean for two distinct groups of developers: those who code for stable employment and those who code as a core part of their identity. For the former, LLMs represent a brutal displacement threat as management uses AI to justify mass layoffs and deskilling. For the latter, the craft of writing elegant code is being abstracted away, replaced by describing desired outcomes while AI generates the actual code. Dash argues that coders have historically been less resistant to automation than other creative workers due to open-source culture, existing automation norms, and weak labor organizing traditions. He calls on passionate developers to use these tools to build independent projects rather than ceding the benefits entirely to tech billionaires, noting that 700,000 tech workers have already been laid off with more to come.

recent_posts.title: MacBook Neo is just Apple rebranding its existing Walmart laptop
recent_posts.summary: Apple's MacBook Neo is a $500-600 brightly-colored laptop being celebrated as a bold new entry into the low-end market, but it's nearly identical in specs to the M1 MacBook Air Apple has been selling at Walmart for years. The Neo's real purpose is brand rehabilitation: Apple needed a way to sell an affordable laptop without the stigma of an old chip number and a Walmart-only distribution channel. The Neo repackages the same hardware with new colors, a distinct visual identity, and marketing aimed at first-time laptop buyers and students. The tech press largely missed this because they don't pay attention to what's been sitting in Walmart's electronics section for years.

recent_posts.title: Apple's video podcast move threatens the open standard that keeps podcasting free
recent_posts.summary: Apple is adding video podcast support to its Podcasts app, but requiring creators to use a small set of pre-approved commercial hosting providers rather than allowing self-hosted video. This breaks with podcasting's foundational open-standard model — the same model that has kept podcasts free from algorithmic manipulation, surveillance advertising, and platform lock-in. The author argues this shift risks enshittifying podcasting the same way social media and streaming platforms have been corrupted. Apple could mitigate this by supporting a fallback open video specification alongside its approved partners, preserving the decentralized nature that makes podcasting uniquely resistant to censorship and corporate capture.
